notes.summary: This chapter covers limits (algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic, 1^∞ forms, limits at infinity), continuity (including piecewise and greatest-integer functions) and differentiability, together with differentiation techniques such as the chain rule, logarithmic and parametric differentiation. JEE Main tests standard-limit manipulation, parameter values for continuity or differentiability, counting points of discontinuity, and quick derivatives.
keyPoints: Standard limits as x → 0: sin x/x = 1, tan x/x = 1, (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2, (eˣ − 1)/x = 1, (aˣ − 1)/x = logₑ a, logₑ(1 + x)/x = 1. As x → a: (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹.
Degrees must be converted to radians: x° = πx/180, so lim (x → 0) sin x°/x = π/180.
Rational functions as x → ∞: compare the highest powers; equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients, e.g. (3x² + …)/(5x² + …) → 3/5.
1^∞ form: lim f^g = e^(lim g(f − 1)), e.g. lim (x → 0) (1 + 2x)^(1/x) = e².
Expansions near 0: sin x ≈ x − x³/6, cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2, tan x ≈ x + x³/3, eˣ ≈ 1 + x + x²/2, logₑ(1 + x) ≈ x − x²/2, (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx.
f is continuous at a if LHL = RHL = f(a); differentiable at a if the left and right derivatives are equal and finite. Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not conversely (|x| at 0).
[g(x)] can jump only where g(x) crosses an integer value: [x²] on (0, 2) jumps at x = 1, √2, √3.
A piecewise function joined at x = c: continuity gives one equation and equal one-sided derivatives give the second.
Logarithmic differentiation: y = xˣ gives y' = xˣ(1 + logₑ x). Parametric form: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
A function defined as a limit in n, such as lim (n → ∞) x²ⁿ, must be split into the cases |x| < 1, |x| = 1 and |x| > 1.
traps: Substituting the limiting value directly into 0/0 or 1^∞ forms instead of simplifying first.
Treating sin x° as sin x and forgetting the factor π/180.
Using continuity alone when the question demands differentiability (two conditions are needed).
Counting discontinuities of [g(x)] at integer values of x instead of where g(x) is an integer.
Calling x|x| non-differentiable at 0 merely because it contains a modulus.
notes.examTip: For x → 0 limits that resist algebra, expand every function up to the x² or x³ term — this settles most JEE Main limit questions in under a minute.

questions.explanation:
Divide numerator and denominator by x², the highest power.
(3 + 2/x − 1/x²)/(5 − 4/x²).
As x → ∞, the terms 2/x, 1/x² and 4/x² tend to 0.
Limit = 3/5. (1/4 is the value at x = 0, not at infinity.)

questions.text: The value of lim (x → 0) (sin x°)/x, where x° denotes x degrees, is:
questions.explanation:
Convert to radians: x° = πx/180.
lim sin(πx/180)/x = (π/180) × lim [sin(πx/180)/(πx/180)].
The bracket tends to 1, so the limit = π/180.

Standard limit: lim (x → 0) (aˣ − 1)/x = logₑ a, for a > 0.
Here a = 5, so the limit = logₑ 5 (about 1.609).
(The answer 1 holds only for a = e.)

questions.text: The function f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = ax + b for x > 1 is differentiable at x = 1. The values of a and b are:
questions.explanation:
Continuity at x = 1: f(1) = 1 must equal a(1) + b, so a + b = 1.
Left derivative = 2x at x = 1 = 2; right derivative = a.
Differentiability: a = 2, so b = 1 − 2 = −1.
(a = 1, b = 0 is continuous but has a corner at x = 1.)

questions.text: The number of points in the open interval (0, 2) at which the function f(x) = [x²] is discontinuous, where [·] denotes the greatest integer function, is:
questions.explanation:
[t] jumps exactly when t passes an integer value.
For x in (0, 2), x² runs through (0, 4), crossing the integers 1, 2 and 3.
x² = 1, 2, 3 gives x = 1, √2, √3, all inside (0, 2).
So f is discontinuous at 3 points.

questions.text: If lim (x → 1) (x⁴ − 1)/(x − 1) = lim (x → k) (x³ − k³)/(x² − k²), where k ≠ 0, then k equals:
questions.explanation:
Use lim (x → a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹.
Left side: 4 × 1³ = 4.
Right side: divide numerator and denominator by (x − k): 3k²/(2k) = 3k/2.
3k/2 = 4, so k = 8/3.

questions.text: Which of the following functions is differentiable at x = 0?
questions.explanation:
f(x) = x|x|: f'(0) = lim (h → 0) h|h|/h = lim |h| = 0 from both sides, so it is differentiable.
|x| and |sin x| have left derivative −1 and right derivative +1 at 0 (a corner).
√|x| has derivative tending to ±∞ on either side (a cusp).
So only x|x| is differentiable at x = 0.

questions.text: If y = xˣ for x > 0, then the value of dy/dx at x = e is:
questions.explanation:
Take logs: logₑ y = x logₑ x.
Differentiate: (1/y)(dy/dx) = logₑ x + 1, so dy/dx = xˣ(1 + logₑ x).
At x = e: eᵉ(1 + 1) = 2eᵉ.
(Using only the power rule or only the exponential rule gives eᵉ.)

questions.text: If x = a cos³t and y = a sin³t, then dy/dx is:
questions.explanation:
dx/dt = 3a cos²t × (−sin t) = −3a cos²t sin t.
dy/dt = 3a sin²t cos t.
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = (3a sin²t cos t)/(−3a cos²t sin t) = −sin t/cos t.
dy/dx = −tan t.

questions.text: The value of lim (x → 0) [1 − cos x · √(cos 2x)]/x² is:
questions.explanation:
Split: 1 − cos x·√(cos 2x) = (1 − cos x) + cos x·(1 − √(cos 2x)).
(1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2.
(1 − √(cos 2x))/x² = (1 − cos 2x)/[x²(1 + √(cos 2x))] → 2/2 = 1, and cos x → 1.
Limit = 1/2 + 1 = 3/2.

questions.text: Let f(x) = lim (n → ∞) (x²ⁿ − 1)/(x²ⁿ + 1) for real x. Then f is discontinuous at:
options: no point; f is continuous everywhere
questions.explanation:
If |x| < 1, x²ⁿ → 0, so f(x) = −1.
If |x| > 1, divide by x²ⁿ: (1 − x⁻²ⁿ)/(1 + x⁻²ⁿ) → 1, so f(x) = 1.
If |x| = 1, x²ⁿ = 1, so f(x) = 0.
f jumps from −1 to 0 to 1 at x = ±1 and is constant elsewhere, so it is discontinuous only at x = −1 and x = 1.
